In brief

Parody. "— Let me, said he, so far presume upon our acquaintance which, however slight it may appear if judged by the standard of mere time, is founded, as I hope and believe, on a sentiment of mutual esteem [...] an emotion whose poignancy, were I to give vent to my feelings, would deprive me even of speech": the Cyclops send-ups turn away from newspaper writing to imitate what sounds like the prose of some elegant urbane fiction. In it, Bob Doran's mawkishly sentimental drunken commiserations become a model of the decorously restrained discourse that 18th century writers called "polite."

At more length

The Enlightenment cult of politeness promoted civility through respectful diplomatic language that could prevent listeners from taking offense at a speaker's churlish, opinionated, disturbingly emotional, or overly famliar sentiments. It grew out of earlier cultural ideals like "courtesy" and "gentility" that were associated with aristocratic behavior, but "politeness" evolved in urban environments where different classes were mingling and social mobility was becoming more the rule than the exception. Phrases like "your most obedient servant" undermined class distinctions, suggesting that in this new world even bourgeois men and women might command the respect previously due to lords and merit deferential bows. Rather than rudely broaching a topic one might tactfully begin, "Pray, good sir, if I may be so bold..." Meeting someone new, one might considerately inquire, "How do you do? I am heartily glad to make your acquaintance."

Joseph Addison and Richard Steele urged politeness on their readers in The Spectator (1711-12), and it played a major role in the novels of "sentiment" and "sensibility" that proliferated several decades later. Gifford supposes that Joyce is parodying "the dialogue in sentimental-genteel nineteenth-century fiction" (Terence Killeen parrots him, detecting "the style of genteel nineteenth-century fiction"), but 18th century novels pioneereed this style, and Enlightenment-era writers were more keenly mindful than Romantics and Victorians of the coarse behavioral realities that polite language covered over. In Tom Jones (1749), for instance, models of decorous human decency like Tom's guardian Squire Allworthy live amidst a human stew of lascivious sexual encounters, noisy eating and drinking, naked greed and resentment, violent outrages, and coarse country manners. Joyce does not echo Fielding or any other single writer, but his parody draws its energy from this kind of stark contrast between coarse reality and elegant discourse.

Let me, says Doran, "presume upon our acquaintance" which, because so recent, may seem "slight"—I didn't know you from Adam before you walked into the bar. Our relationship is built on "mutual esteem"—surely you admire anonymous slobbering barhounds. If I "have overstepped the limits of reserve" it is because of "the sincerity of my feelings"—when I'm this far gone in drink my tongue starts moving of its own accord there's no telling what may spew from my mouth.

No, says Bloom, "I appreciate to the full the motives which actuate your conduct"—I can see quite clearly that you're blind drunk and not in control of your mouth. "I shall discharge the office you entrust to me," knowing that it "sweetens in some measure the bitterness of the cup"—telling Mrs. Dignam that some unknown drunkard complimented her drunkard husband "Willy" is sure to lessen her grief and ameliorate the awkwardness of our meeting.

Then "suffer me to take your hand," says Doran—the narrator has observed the grotesque spectacle of him "shaking Bloom's hand doing the tragic." The "goodness of your heart," he trusts, will suggest to you suitable words for conveying "an emotion whose poignancy, were I to give vent to my feelings, would deprive me even of speech"—if I emote any more I'm likely to pass out.

This parody leaves behind the mockery of specifically Irish pretensions, but it continues to advance the absurd fantasy that Barney Kiernan's is a place of high cultural accomplishment.

John Hunt 2026
